6: # URDF
7: 
8: Provenance: maintained in [earthtojake/text-to-cad](https://github.com/earthtojake/text-to-cad).
9: Use the installed local skill files as the runtime source of truth; the
10: repository link is only for provenance and release review.
11: 
12: Use this skill for URDF robot-description outputs. Treat URDF work as constrained kinematic modeling, not just XML writing. The main correctness risks are frame placement, joint-axis semantics, unit consistency, mesh scale, and inertial data.
13: 
14: ## Core Rules
15: 
16: 1. The `.urdf` file is the source of truth. Author and edit URDF XML directly; do not build a Python generation pipeline for it. There is no `gen_urdf()` contract.
17: 2. Before writing or changing URDF XML, establish the robot's frame, joint, geometry, unit, and assumption ledger and embed it as a comment block at the top of the `.urdf` file. See `references/design-ledger.md`.
18: 3. Use URDF frame semantics exactly. Joint origins, link frames, joint axes, and visual/collision/inertial origins use different reference frames. See `references/frame-semantics.md`.
19: 4. Do not infer spatial transforms, mesh units, handedness, axes, or joint signs from vague prose. Use CAD transforms, dimensioned drawings, measured values, existing source data, or explicit documented assumptions.
20: 5. Never freehand numeric values that are the result of computation — inertia tensors, centers of mass, unit conversions across many links, mirrored transforms. Compute them: closed-form formulas for primitives, or a throwaway helper script for mesh-derived values. See `references/inertials.md`.
21: 6. For physical links, model `inertial`, `visual`, and `collision` separately when the target consumer needs them. Frame-only links may intentionally omit mass and geometry.
22: 7. Validate every created or modified `.urdf` with `scripts/validate` before reporting completion. See `references/validation.md`.
23: 8. Helper scripts are allowed and encouraged for computation, but they are scaffolding, not the artifact's source of truth. For complex or genuinely parametric models it is reasonable to keep a model-local helper script on disk next to related source code (for example STEP generator sources) and note it in the ledger; this is optional, and the checked-in `.urdf` remains canonical.
24: 
25: ## CAD Viewer Handoff
26: 
27: After completing URDF work that creates or modifies a `.urdf`, you must ALWAYS hand the explicit file path to `$cad-viewer` when that skill is installed. `$cad-viewer` must start CAD Viewer if it is not already running and return link(s) to the relevant created or updated file(s); if `$cad-viewer` is unavailable or startup fails, report that instead of silently omitting the handoff.
28: 
29: ## Workflow
30: 
31: 1. Identify the target `.urdf` file and its consumers: RViz, robot_state_publisher, Gazebo/Ignition, MoveIt, a real robot driver, or another simulator.
32: 2. Read or create the design ledger before editing frames, origins, axes, mesh scale, limits, or inertials. Keep the ledger as a comment block in the `.urdf` itself.
33: 3. Prepare mesh assets first when links reference meshes: one mesh per link, exported in that link's frame by the owning CAD/mesh workflow. See `references/meshes.md`.
34: 4. Author or edit the URDF XML directly, following `references/authoring-contract.md` for structure, ordering, and naming.
35: 5. Compute — never guess — inertials and other derived numbers. See `references/inertials.md`.
36: 6. Validate with `scripts/validate`; fix findings and re-validate until clean.
37: 7. Run the verification recipe in `references/validation.md`: external tools when available (`check_urdf`), then a viewer review sweeping every joint.
38: 8. Report remaining assumptions, unchecked spatial data, and validation gaps.
39: 
40: ## Commands
41: 
42: Run with the Python environment for the project or workspace. Treat `python` in examples as an interpreter placeholder; if bare `python` is unavailable, substitute `python3`, a project virtualenv interpreter, or the configured interpreter path. The validator uses only the Python standard library.
43: 
44: From this skill directory, the validator shape is:
45: 
46: ```bash
47: python scripts/validate path/to/robot.urdf
48: python scripts/validate path/to/a.urdf path/to/b.urdf
49: python scripts/validate path/to/robot.urdf --strict
50: python scripts/validate path/to/robot.urdf --format json
51: python scripts/validate path/to/robot.urdf --package robot_description=/path/to/pkg
52: ```
53: 
54: The validator collects all findings in one pass (severity, code, XML path) across XML structure, tree topology, joint semantics (limits, mimic, dynamics), geometry, mesh references, materials, inertial physics, and misspelled elements, and prints a per-file summary. `--strict` treats warnings as failures; `--format json` emits a machine-readable findings document; `--package NAME=PATH` resolves `package://` mesh URIs. It exits nonzero if any target fails. Relative targets resolve from the current working directory; when running from outside this skill directory, prefix the launcher path so target files still resolve from the intended workspace.
55: 
56: Validation is a guardrail, not spatial proof: a URDF can pass every structural check while placing a joint in the wrong spot. The ledger and viewer sweep exist for that reason.
57: 
58: ## Snapshot Tool
59: 
60: `scripts/snapshot` renders the robot to a PNG still or an orbit GIF, using the same shared
61: CLI and headless browser runtime every rendering skill uses — so a snapshot matches what
62: the CAD Viewer shows.
63: 
64: ```bash
65: python scripts/snapshot --input path/to/robot.urdf --output review.png
66: python scripts/snapshot --input path/to/robot.urdf --output turntable.gif --mode orbit
67: ```
68: 
69: It accepts `.urdf` only. Pose the robot with the job field `"jointValues"` (joint name to
70: degrees, defaulting to the rest pose) rather than `--params`, which is STEP-only; robots
71: are authored in metres and are framed on the robot scene scale automatically.
72: 
73: Theme settings live under one `--theme`, mirroring the viewer's Theme tab. The default
74: theme is `snapshot` — Workbench Light with the ground grid, origin axis and shadows
75: removed, because in a still image those read as geometry. There is no `--display`: display
76: settings (mode, clip, exploded, edges) are CAD topology settings, and a robot carries none.
77: 
78: Link meshes are resolved relative to the description, so they must be present: an
79: unhydrated Git LFS pointer fails as "No link mesh loaded for robot". Run
80: `git lfs checkout <mesh dir>` first.
81: 
82: Use `python scripts/snapshot --help` for the complete current command interface.

2: 
3: Use this reference when writing or editing URDF XML directly. The `.urdf` file is the source of truth: it must carry its own documentation, and its structure must be predictable enough that any later agent or engineer can audit it without external context.
4: 
5: ## File Shape
6: 
7: Every authored `.urdf` follows this shape, in this order:
8: 
9: 1. XML declaration: `<?xml version="1.0"?>`.
10: 2. Design-ledger comment block (see below).
11: 3. One `<robot name="...">` root element.
12: 4. All `<link>` elements, root link first, then in tree order (parents before children).
13: 5. All `<joint>` elements, in the same tree order as the child links they create.
14: 
15: Keep two-space indentation and one element per line. Do not interleave links and joints arbitrarily; a reader should be able to walk the kinematic tree top-to-bottom.
16: 
17: ## Design-Ledger Comment Block
18: 
19: The ledger lives in the file, immediately after the XML declaration, as XML comments. Minimum content:
20: 
21: ```xml
22: <?xml version="1.0"?>
23: <!--
24:   robot: <name> | consumers: <RViz / Gazebo / MoveIt / driver / viewer>
25:   units: meters, kilograms, radians | frames: +X forward, +Y left, +Z up (REP-103)
26:   root: <root_link> | source of dimensions: <CAD file / drawing / measured / assumption>
27:   meshes: <dir>, exported per-link in link frame, source units <mm|m>, scale <...>
28:   inertials: <CAD mass properties / primitive formulas / assumed density X kg/m^3 / omitted>
29:   assumptions: <every guessed value, sign convention, or approximation, one per line>
30: -->
31: ```
32: 
33: Update the ledger in the same edit that changes the modeled facts. A stale ledger is worse than no ledger. See `references/design-ledger.md` for the full ledger checklist.
34: 
35: ## Naming
36: 
37: - Links: `<part>_link` for physical links (`base_link`, `forearm_link`), bare descriptive names for frame-only links (`base_footprint`, `tool0`, `camera_optical_frame`).
38: - Joints: `<child-function>_joint` or `<parent>_to_<child>` (`shoulder_pan_joint`, `wrist_roll`). One convention per file.
39: - Names are identifiers consumed by SRDF, controllers, and TF; never rename casually. If a rename is required, update every consumer (SRDF groups, group states, disabled collisions) in the same task.
40: 
41: ## Element Contract
42: 
43: For every `<link>` that represents physical geometry, author the subelements in this order: `inertial`, `visual`, `collision`. Frame-only links are empty (`<link name="tool0" />`) and must be listed as frame-only in the ledger.
44: 
45: For every `<joint>`:
46: 
47: - Attributes: `name`, `type` (`fixed`, `revolute`, `continuous`, or `prismatic`; use `floating`/`planar` only when the consumer and validation path support them — the bundled validator rejects them).
48: - Children in order: `<parent>`, `<child>`, `<origin>`, `<axis>` (movable joints), `<limit>` (revolute/prismatic), then optional `<dynamics>`, `<mimic>`, `<calibration>`, `<safety_controller>`.
49: - `<origin>` is the parent-link-frame transform to the joint frame at zero position; the child link frame coincides with the joint frame.
50: - `<axis>` is expressed in the joint (child) frame and should be a signed unit vector along a principal axis whenever the mechanism allows (`1 0 0`, `0 -1 0`, ...). A non-principal axis is a red flag: re-check the frame definitions before accepting one.
51: - `<limit>` carries radians (revolute) or meters (prismatic) plus `effort` and `velocity` when the consumer needs them. `continuous` joints take no lower/upper limits.
52: 
53: Never encode a kinematic fix by offsetting only the visual mesh; correct the joint/link frames instead, unless the mesh is genuinely offset from the link frame.
54: 
55: ## Golden Skeleton

2: 
3: Use this reference before creating or editing a `.urdf`. The ledger is the written spatial model that prevents silent frame, axis, unit, and mesh-scale mistakes.
4: 
5: The ledger's canonical home is a comment block at the top of the `.urdf` file itself (see the compact format in `references/authoring-contract.md`), optionally expanded in an adjacent README for large robots. It must be specific enough that another engineer can audit the URDF without reverse-engineering the XML, and it must be updated in the same edit that changes the modeled facts.
6: 
7: The sections below are the checklist of what the ledger must cover. For small robots the per-link and per-joint tables can collapse into a few comment lines; the information, not the table format, is what is required.
8: 
9: ## Required Sections
10: 
11: ### Robot Metadata
12: 
13: Record:
14: 
15: - robot name
16: - target consumers: RViz, robot_state_publisher, Gazebo/Ignition, MoveIt, real robot driver, or other
17: - unit convention: meters, kilograms, seconds, radians unless the project explicitly states otherwise
18: - frame convention: REP-103-style body convention when applicable, or a documented exception
19: - mesh unit convention: meters, millimeters, inches, or other
20: - source of dimensions: CAD, drawing, measured data, vendor documentation, existing URDF, or assumption
21: 
22: ### Link Ledger
23: 
24: For every link, record:
25: 
26: | Field | Meaning |
27: |---|---|
28: | link name | Exact URDF `<link name="...">` value. |
29: | role | Physical link, frame-only link, sensor frame, tool frame, base frame, or other. |
30: | frame definition | Where the link frame is located and how its axes point. |
31: | parent joint | Joint that creates this child link frame, or `none` for root. |
32: | visual geometry | Primitive or mesh source, with origin relative to the link frame. |
33: | collision geometry | Primitive or mesh source, with origin relative to the link frame. |
34: | inertial source | CAD mass properties, vendor data, approximation, or intentionally omitted. |
35: 
36: Frame-only links such as `base_footprint`, optical frames, and `tool0` may omit inertial, visual, and collision blocks. Mark them explicitly as frame-only rather than leaving intent ambiguous.
37: 
38: ### Joint Ledger
39: 
40: For every joint, record:
41: 
42: | Field | Meaning |
43: |---|---|
44: | joint name | Exact URDF `<joint name="...">` value. |
45: | type | `fixed`, `revolute`, `continuous`, or `prismatic` for the bundled validator; record `floating` or `planar` only if the project has a different supported validation path. |
46: | parent link | Link whose frame expresses the joint origin. |
47: | child link | Link whose frame is created at the joint frame. |
48: | origin xyz/rpy | Parent-link-frame transform from parent link to joint frame. |
49: | axis | Axis vector expressed in the joint frame, for movable joints. |
50: | limits | Radians for revolute, meters for prismatic, no finite lower/upper limits for continuous. |
51: | positive motion | What positive joint motion physically does. |
52: | source | CAD, drawing, measured data, existing model, or documented assumption. |
53: 
54: Do not write a movable joint without an explicit positive-motion convention. The sign of the axis is part of the model, not a cosmetic detail.
55: 
56: ### Geometry Ledger
57: 
58: For every visual or collision item, record:
59: 
60: | Field | Meaning |
61: |---|---|
62: | link | Owning link. |
63: | kind | `visual` or `collision`. |
64: | geometry type | `mesh`, `box`, `cylinder`, or `sphere`. |
65: | source | CAD export, primitive approximation, vendor mesh, generated mesh, or temporary placeholder. |
66: | origin xyz/rpy | Transform from link frame to geometry frame. |
67: | scale | Mesh scale if applicable. |
68: | units | Mesh source units and URDF scale needed to express meters. |
69: 
70: Visual geometry is for display. Collision geometry is for contact, planning, and physics. It may intentionally be simpler than the visual geometry.
71: 
72: ### Inertial Ledger
73: 
74: For every physical link, record:
75: 
76: | Field | Meaning |
77: |---|---|
78: | mass | Kilograms. |
79: | center of mass | Inertial origin xyz in the link frame. |
80: | inertia tensor | Tensor values and frame. |
81: | source | CAD mass properties, vendor data, calculation, approximation, or intentionally omitted. |
82: | confidence | Exact, estimated, placeholder, or unknown. |
83: 
84: Do not silently copy visual origins into inertial origins. The visual frame, collision frame, link frame, and center of mass can all differ.
85: 
86: ### Assumption Ledger
87: 
88: Record every inferred or guessed value, including:
89: 
90: - unknown dimensions
91: - mesh units
92: - sign conventions
93: - joint axes
94: - parent/child direction
95: - visual or collision offsets
96: - mass, COM, and inertia approximations
97: - frame-only link intent
98: - unverified package URI resolution
99: 
100: List assumptions one per line in the ledger comment block so they survive with the file. In helper scripts, name assumed values by physical meaning (`ASSUMED_BASE_TO_SHOULDER_Z_M`), never as unlabelled numeric literals.
101: 
102: ## When Information Is Missing
103: 
104: If spatial information is missing, do not invent a precise-looking transform. Choose one of these outcomes:
105: 
106: 1. preserve existing source data unchanged;
107: 2. create a frame-only or placeholder structure with explicit assumption comments;
108: 3. use a clearly named approximate constant;
109: 4. ask for dimensions or CAD data when the workflow allows interaction;
110: 5. report that the model is structurally valid but spatially provisional.
